decks.title: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Benzene — Part 1: Structure, aromaticity, preparation and properties
goals: Name benzene derivatives by the IUPAC system, using ortho, meta, para and numbering
Describe the structure of benzene by Kekulé structures and resonance, and explain its stability with hydrogenation data
Apply Hückel's rule to decide whether a ring is aromatic
Prepare benzene from sodium benzoate and from phenol, and state its physical properties

slides.heading: Benzene and the aromatic hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: **Aromatic hydrocarbons (arenes)** contain a benzene ring or a ring with similar properties. **Benzene, C₆H₆**, is the parent. It is a planar, cyclic molecule with a **delocalised π system**, so it behaves very differently from the alkenes it seems to resemble: it prefers **substitution** to addition.

rows: Six-carbon ring, one H on each carbon

visual.alt: Table of four aromatic hydrocarbons with formula and a description of the structure

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on benzene. Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring or a ring that behaves in the same way. Benzene is the parent compound. It is a flat ring of six carbon atoms with a delocalised system of pi electrons. This makes it very different from the alkenes: it prefers substitution to addition. In this part we study its naming, structure, aromaticity, preparation and physical properties.

slides.heading: Naming monosubstituted benzenes
slides.body_md: Most monosubstituted compounds are named **substituent + benzene**: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene. Some keep **parent names** that include the group: **phenol** (–OH), **aniline** (aminobenzene, –NH₂), **benzoic acid** (–COOH), **benzaldehyde** (–CHO), **toluene** (methylbenzene) and **styrene** (ethenylbenzene). **C₆H₅–** is the **phenyl** group; **C₆H₅CH₂–** is **benzyl**.

visual.alt: Table of six monosubstituted benzenes with structural formula, IUPAC name and common name

slides.narration: A simple derivative is named by writing the substituent followed by benzene, as in chlorobenzene or nitrobenzene. Some compounds keep special names that include the functional group. Hydroxybenzene is phenol, aminobenzene is aniline, and the benzene ring carrying a carboxylic acid group is benzoic acid. The group made of a benzene ring minus one hydrogen is called phenyl, and the group with an extra methylene is called benzyl.

slides.heading: Ortho, meta, para and numbering
slides.body_md: Two groups on a ring are **1,2 (ortho, o-)**, **1,3 (meta, m-)** or **1,4 (para, p-)**. With three or more substituents, **number** the ring to give the **lowest locants**; cite substituents **alphabetically**. If the ring carries a group that gives a parent name (phenol, benzoic acid, aniline), that carbon is **C-1**.

CH₃ and NO₂ on carbons 1 and 4
Br and NO₂ on carbons 1 and 3

COOH at C-1, Br at C-2, NO₂ at C-4

slides.narration: When there are two substituents, the positions one and two are called ortho, one and three are meta, and one and four are para. With three or more groups, number the ring so that the locants are as low as possible and cite the substituents in alphabetical order. If one group gives a parent name, such as phenol or benzoic acid, that carbon is number one and the other groups are numbered from it.

slides.heading: Structure of benzene: Kekulé structures and resonance
slides.body_md: Kekulé proposed a six-membered ring with **alternating single and double bonds**. Two such structures exist, differing only in the **positions of the double bonds**. Neither is correct alone: benzene is a **resonance hybrid** of both. All six C–C bonds are **equal (139 pm)**, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm), and the ring is a **regular planar hexagon** (all angles 120°).

slides.narration: Kekulé suggested a ring of six carbons with alternate single and double bonds. Two such structures can be drawn, differing only in where the double bonds are placed. Neither alone describes benzene. The real molecule is a resonance hybrid of the two. All six carbon carbon bonds are identical, with a length between that of a single and a double bond, and the ring is a flat regular hexagon with all bond angles one hundred and twenty degrees.

slides.heading: The delocalised π cloud of benzene
slides.body_md: Each carbon is **sp² hybridised**: three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) in one plane, and one **p orbital perpendicular to the ring**. The six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring, so the **six π electrons are delocalised** in two ring-shaped clouds above and below the plane. Benzene has **12 σ bonds** and six delocalised π electrons.

slides.narration: In the orbital picture, each carbon is sp two hybridised. Three hybrid orbitals form sigma bonds in the plane of the ring. The fourth orbital, a p orbital, stands at right angles to the ring. The six p orbitals overlap sideways all the way round, so the six pi electrons are not held between particular pairs of carbons but are delocalised in two ring shaped clouds, one above and one below the plane of the ring.

slides.heading: Evidence for the structure and stability of benzene
slides.body_md: A single Kekulé triene would behave like an alkene with three isolated C=C bonds. Benzene does not: it **does not decolourise bromine water** or acidified KMnO₄ under ordinary conditions, gives **only one** monosubstituted product and **only one** 1,2-disubstituted product, has **equal C–C lengths**, and is **far more stable** than the triene (its hydrogenation is much less exothermic).

visual.alt: Table comparing five observations for an isolated triene with those found for benzene

slides.narration: If benzene were a simple triene it would behave like an alkene with three isolated double bonds, but it does not. It does not decolourise bromine water or permanganate under ordinary conditions. It gives only one monosubstituted product and only one product with two neighbouring substituents. All its carbon carbon bonds are equal in length. And it is far more stable than expected, as its heat of hydrogenation shows.

slides.heading: Resonance energy from hydrogenation data
slides.body_md: Hydrogenating **cyclohexene** releases **120 kJ mol⁻¹**. A hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene would release 3 × 120 = **360 kJ mol⁻¹**, but benzene releases only **208 kJ mol⁻¹**. Benzene is therefore **152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable** than the triene: the **resonance (delocalisation) energy, about 150 kJ mol⁻¹**.

slides.narration: The extra stability of benzene can be measured. Hydrogenation of cyclohexene releases one hundred and twenty kilojoules per mole. A triene with three separate double bonds should therefore release three hundred and sixty. Benzene releases only two hundred and eight. The difference, one hundred and fifty two kilojoules per mole, is the resonance energy. It is the extra stability that comes from delocalisation of the pi electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: resonance energy
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The enthalpies of hydrogenation to cyclohexane are: cyclohexene −120 kJ mol⁻¹, cyclohexa-1,3-diene −232 kJ mol⁻¹ and benzene −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Find the stabilisation of each of the last two relative to isolated C=C bonds.

**Solution.** Benzene: expected 3 × (−120) = −360; observed −208; stabilisation = −208 − (−360) = **152 kJ mol⁻¹**. Cyclohexa-1,3-diene: expected 2 × (−120) = −240; observed −232; stabilisation = −232 − (−240) = **8 kJ mol⁻¹**. Delocalisation over a ring of six π electrons is far more stabilising than over a simple conjugated diene.

visual.alt: Table of expected and observed enthalpies of hydrogenation and the stabilisation of cyclohexa-1,3-diene and benzene

slides.narration: For each compound, multiply the cyclohexene value by the number of double bonds to get the expected heat release, then subtract it from the observed value. For the diene the difference is small, only a few kilojoules per mole. For benzene it is one hundred and fifty two. So the extra stability of benzene is not just the effect of two double bonds being conjugated, but the special stability of the closed ring of six delocalised electrons.

slides.heading: Aromaticity and Hückel's rule
slides.body_md: A compound is **aromatic** if its ring is **planar, cyclic, fully conjugated** (a continuous ring of p orbitals) and has **(4n + 2) π electrons** (n = 0, 1, 2, …): 2, 6, 10, … (**Hückel's rule**). With **4n** π electrons a planar ring is **antiaromatic** and unstable. Non-planar rings such as cyclooctatetraene are not aromatic.

visual.alt: Table applying Hückel rule to six ring compounds with pi electron count, planarity and verdict

slides.narration: Aromatic compounds follow Hückel rule. The ring must be flat, cyclic and fully conjugated, with a continuous ring of p orbitals, and it must contain four n plus two pi electrons, where n is zero or a whole number. Benzene has six and naphthalene has ten. A flat ring with four n electrons, such as cyclobutadiene, is antiaromatic and unstable. Cyclooctatetraene is tub shaped, so it is not conjugated all round and is not aromatic.

slides.heading: Worked example: using Hückel's rule
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Decide whether (a) the cyclopentadienyl cation C₅H₅⁺, (b) the cyclopentadienyl anion C₅H₅⁻ and (c) the tropylium cation C₇H₇⁺ are aromatic, if each is planar with a ring of p orbitals.

**Solution.** Count the π electrons. (a) Four sp² carbons each give one π electron, and the fifth, a carbocation, gives none, so **4** π electrons: this is 4n (n = 1), **antiaromatic**. (b) The extra negative charge adds a pair: 4 + 2 = **6** π electrons = 4n + 2 (n = 1): **aromatic**. (c) Seven carbons with a + charge: 7 − 1 = **6** π electrons: **aromatic**.

visual.alt: Table of three ring ions with ring size, pi electron count and verdict

slides.narration: Count the pi electrons in each ring. The cyclopentadienyl cation has four, which fits four n and makes it antiaromatic. The anion has gained an electron pair, giving six, which fits four n plus two with n equal to one, so it is aromatic. The tropylium cation has seven ring carbons but one of them has no electron because of the positive charge, so there are six pi electrons and the ion is aromatic.

slides.heading: Physical properties of benzene
slides.body_md: Benzene is a **colourless, mobile liquid** with a characteristic smell, **insoluble in water** (it floats, density 0.879 g mL⁻¹) but miscible with organic solvents; it is itself a good solvent. It is non-polar (zero dipole moment). It burns with a **sooty flame** (92.3% carbon). Its **high melting point** (5.5 °C) compared with methylbenzene (−95 °C) reflects its **symmetry**, which allows close packing in the crystal; likewise p-xylene melts higher than o- and m-xylene.

slides.narration: Benzene is a colourless liquid with a characteristic smell. It does not mix with water and floats on it, but it mixes with organic solvents and is itself a good solvent. It is non polar. It burns with a sooty flame because of its high carbon content. Its melting point is much higher than that of methylbenzene because the symmetrical molecules pack closely in the crystal. In the same way, para xylene melts higher than its ortho and meta isomers.

slides.heading: Preparation of benzene
slides.body_md: **From sodium benzoate:** heating with **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO) removes the carboxyl group (**decarboxylation**): $\ce{C6H5COONa + NaOH -> C6H6 + Na2CO3}$. **From phenol:** phenol vapour is passed over **heated zinc dust**, which removes the oxygen as zinc oxide: $\ce{C6H5OH + Zn -> C6H6 + ZnO}$. (Benzene is also formed by passing ethyne through a red-hot iron tube.)

slides.narration: Benzene can be prepared in the laboratory in two ways. Sodium benzoate is heated with soda lime, a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide. The carboxylate group is lost as carbonate, which is called decarboxylation. Alternatively, phenol vapour is passed over heated zinc dust. The zinc removes the oxygen as zinc oxide, and benzene is formed. Benzene is also obtained from ethyne in a red hot iron tube.

slides.heading: Why benzene undergoes substitution
slides.body_md: Addition would destroy the **delocalised π system** and lose about **150 kJ mol⁻¹** of resonance energy, whereas **substitution keeps the ring intact**. The π cloud also attracts **electrophiles**, so the typical reaction of benzene is **electrophilic substitution**: an H is replaced by an electrophile E⁺.

visual.alt: Table comparing the reactions of cyclohexene and benzene with four reagents

slides.narration: Addition would destroy the delocalised pi system and lose the resonance energy of about one hundred and fifty kilojoules per mole. Substitution keeps the ring intact, so it is the typical reaction of benzene. The pi cloud above and below the ring attracts electron seeking species, called electrophiles, so the usual reaction is electrophilic substitution, in which a hydrogen is replaced by an electrophile.

slides.heading: Mechanism of electrophilic substitution: nitration
slides.body_md: Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ (323–333 K) makes the **nitronium ion NO₂⁺**: $\ce{HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-}$. **Step 1 (slow):** the π electrons attack NO₂⁺, forming the **arenium ion (σ complex)**, a resonance-stabilised carbocation with the + shared by C-2, C-4, C-6. **Step 2 (fast):** loss of H⁺ restores the aromatic ring, giving **nitrobenzene**. Every electrophilic substitution follows this two-step pattern.

slides.narration: Here is the mechanism of nitration. Concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid form the nitronium ion, the electrophile. In the slow first step, the pi electrons of benzene attack the nitronium ion, forming the arenium ion, a carbocation whose positive charge is spread over three carbons by resonance. In the fast second step, a proton is lost from the carbon that bears the nitro group, the ring becomes aromatic again, and nitrobenzene is formed.

slides.heading: Halogenation and sulphonation
slides.body_md: **Halogenation:** Cl₂ or Br₂ with a Lewis acid (**FeCl₃ or FeBr₃**, or iron), in the dark, gives **chlorobenzene** or **bromobenzene**: $\ce{C6H6 + Cl2 ->[FeCl3] C6H5Cl + HCl}$; the catalyst polarises the halogen to make the electrophile. **Sulphonation:** conc. H₂SO₄ or **oleum** (electrophile **SO₃**) gives **benzenesulphonic acid**: $\ce{C6H6 + H2SO4 -> C6H5SO3H + H2O}$. Sulphonation is **reversible**: heating with dilute acid or steam removes the –SO₃H group.

visual.alt: Table of halogenation and sulphonation of benzene with reagents, electrophile and product

slides.narration: In halogenation, chlorine or bromine reacts with benzene in the presence of an iron halide catalyst, in the dark, and chlorobenzene or bromobenzene is formed. The catalyst polarises the halogen molecule to make the electrophile. Sulphonation uses concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum, and the electrophile is sulphur trioxide. The product is benzenesulphonic acid. Sulphonation is reversible, so the sulphonic acid group can be removed again by heating with dilute acid or steam.

slides.heading: Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation
slides.body_md: **Alkylation:** an alkyl halide with **anhydrous AlCl₃** gives an alkylbenzene, e.g. $\ce{C6H6 + CH3Cl ->[AlCl3] C6H5CH3 + HCl}$; the electrophile is a **carbocation** (R⁺). Limits: **polyalkylation** (the alkyl group activates the ring) and **rearrangement** of the carbocation. **Acylation:** an acyl chloride with AlCl₃ gives a **ketone**: $\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$ (phenylethanone); the electrophile is the **acylium ion CH₃CO⁺**, and the product is deactivated, so **no further acylation** occurs.

visual.alt: Friedel-Crafts acylation: benzene with ethanoyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride gives phenylethanone and hydrogen chloride
visual.caption: Friedel–Crafts acylation

slides.narration: In Friedel Crafts alkylation, benzene reacts with an alkyl halide in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride, and the electrophile is a carbocation. The alkyl group activates the ring, so more than one alkyl group may enter, and the carbocation may rearrange. In Friedel Crafts acylation, an acid chloride with aluminium chloride gives a ketone through the acylium ion. The ketone group deactivates the ring, so the reaction stops after one substitution.

slides.heading: The five electrophilic substitutions at a glance
slides.body_md: In each case the ring keeps its **six π electrons** and one **H is replaced** by the electrophile. Memorise the **reagent and the electrophile**: Cl⁺ (Cl₂/FeCl₃), **NO₂⁺**, **SO₃**, **R⁺** and **RCO⁺** (with AlCl₃). Friedel–Crafts reactions need **anhydrous** conditions because AlCl₃ reacts with water.

slides.narration: This diagram collects the five substitutions. In each, the ring keeps its six pi electrons and one hydrogen is replaced. Halogenation uses a halogen and an iron halide, nitration uses concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids, sulphonation uses concentrated sulphuric acid or oleum, and the two Friedel Crafts reactions use an alkyl halide or an acid chloride with anhydrous aluminium chloride. These conditions must be dry, because aluminium chloride reacts with water.

slides.heading: Worked example: yield of nitrobenzene
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 11.7 g of benzene is nitrated with excess mixed acid and the yield of nitrobenzene is 70.0%. Find the mass of nitrobenzene obtained and the minimum mass of HNO₃ needed. (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)

**Solution.** $\ce{C6H6 + HNO3 -> C6H5NO2 + H2O}$, 1 : 1 : 1. n(C₆H₆) = 11.7 ÷ 78 = 0.150 mol. Theoretical mass of C₆H₅NO₂ = 0.150 × 123 = 18.45 g; at 70.0% yield: 18.45 × 70.0/100 = **12.9 g**. Minimum HNO₃ = 0.150 × 63 = **9.45 g**.

visual.alt: Table of moles of benzene, theoretical and actual mass of nitrobenzene and minimum mass of nitric acid

slides.narration: Write the balanced equation first. One mole of benzene gives one mole of nitrobenzene and needs one mole of nitric acid. The molar mass of benzene is seventy eight, so the sample is point one five zero mole. Multiplying by the molar mass of nitrobenzene gives the theoretical mass. The actual mass is that figure multiplied by the percentage yield. The minimum mass of nitric acid is the moles multiplied by sixty three.

slides.heading: Directive influence of substituents
slides.body_md: A group already on the ring decides **where** the next electrophile enters and **how fast**. **Ortho/para directors** (and activating) donate electrons: **–OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃, –CH₃ and other alkyl groups**. The **halogens** are ortho/para directing but **deactivating**. **Meta directors** (deactivating) withdraw electrons: **–NO₂, –CN, –COOH, –CHO, –COR, –SO₃H**. Ease of substitution: phenol > methylbenzene > benzene > nitrobenzene.

visual.alt: Table of substituents with electronic effect, directing position and effect on ring reactivity

slides.narration: A group already on the ring controls where the next substituent goes and how fast the reaction is. Groups that donate electrons, such as hydroxyl, amino and alkyl groups, direct to the ortho and para positions and make the ring more reactive. Halogens direct ortho and para but make the ring less reactive. Groups that withdraw electrons, such as nitro, cyano, carboxyl and carbonyl groups, direct to the meta position and make the ring less reactive.

slides.heading: Why? Resonance and product distribution
slides.body_md: **Donor group (CH₃, OH):** for **ortho/para** attack, one resonance form of the arenium ion puts the + **on the carbon bearing the donor**, which stabilises it. **Withdrawing group (NO₂):** for ortho/para attack, that form puts the + **next to the electron-poor N⁺**, which is very unfavourable; **meta** attack avoids it, so meta is the least bad (and the ring is deactivated overall). Experimentally: toluene gives about **58% o, 4% m, 38% p**; nitrobenzene gives about **93% m**.

slides.narration: To explain the directive effect, look at the arenium ion. With a donor group such as methyl, attack at the ortho or para position gives a resonance form in which the positive charge sits on the carbon carrying the donor, which stabilises it. With a withdrawing group such as nitro, the same attack puts the positive charge next to the electron poor nitrogen, which is very unfavourable, so meta attack, which avoids this, is preferred. The product ratios confirm it.

slides.heading: Worked example: predicting the products
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the main products when (a) methylbenzene is brominated with Br₂/FeBr₃ and (b) nitrobenzene is brominated under the same conditions. Which reacts faster than benzene?

**Solution.** (a) –CH₃ is an **ortho/para director and activating**: the products are **2-bromo-1-methylbenzene (o-bromotoluene) and 4-bromo-1-methylbenzene (p-bromotoluene)**; the reaction is **faster than** with benzene. (b) –NO₂ is a **meta director and deactivating**: the product is **1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene**; the reaction is **slower than** with benzene and needs more vigorous conditions.

visual.alt: Table of the bromination of methylbenzene and nitrobenzene with directing effect, main products and rate relative to benzene

slides.narration: First classify the group already on the ring. Methyl donates electrons, so it directs ortho and para and makes the ring more reactive than benzene. The products of bromination are the ortho and para bromomethylbenzenes. The nitro group withdraws electrons, so it directs meta and makes the ring less reactive, and the product is one bromo three nitrobenzene, formed more slowly and under harsher conditions.

slides.heading: Oxidation and ozonolysis of benzene
slides.body_md: The ring resists oxidants: benzene does **not decolourise KMnO₄**. It **burns** with a sooty flame: $\ce{2C6H6 + 15O2 -> 12CO2 + 6H2O}$. Vapour mixed with air over **V₂O₅ at about 773 K** gives **maleic anhydride** (the ring breaks). **Ozonolysis:** benzene adds three O₃ to give a triozonide, which on reduction with Zn and water gives **three molecules of glyoxal** (OHC–CHO): $\ce{C6H6 + 3O3 -> C6H6O9}$, then $\ce{C6H6O9 + 3Zn + 3H2O -> 3OHCCHO + 3Zn(OH)2}$.

visual.alt: Table of the oxidation and ozonolysis products of benzene compared with cyclohexene

slides.narration: The benzene ring resists oxidation, and it does not decolourise potassium permanganate. It burns in air with a sooty flame to give carbon dioxide and water. Vapour passed with air over vanadium pentoxide at about seven hundred and seventy three kelvin is oxidised to maleic anhydride. With ozone, benzene forms a triozonide, and reduction with zinc and water gives three molecules of glyoxal, the dialdehyde ethanedial.

slides.heading: Addition and pyrolysis
slides.body_md: Only under forcing conditions does benzene add reagents. **H₂/Ni, 473 K** gives **cyclohexane**: $\ce{C6H6 + 3H2 -> C6H12}$. **Cl₂ in UV light or sunlight (no catalyst)** adds three Cl₂, giving **benzene hexachloride (BHC, hexachlorocyclohexane)** $\ce{C6H6 + 3Cl2 -> C6H6Cl6}$; Br₂ with UV gives C₆H₆Br₆. **Pyrolysis** (benzene vapour through a red-hot tube) gives **biphenyl**: $\ce{2C6H6 -> C12H10 + H2}$.

slides.narration: Benzene adds reagents only under forcing conditions. With hydrogen and nickel at four hundred and seventy three kelvin it forms cyclohexane. With chlorine in ultraviolet light and no catalyst, three molecules of chlorine add, giving benzene hexachloride, also called hexachlorocyclohexane. Bromine behaves in the same way. When benzene vapour is passed through a red hot tube, two molecules join with loss of hydrogen, and biphenyl is formed.

slides.heading: Hazards, precautions and uses
slides.body_md: Benzene is **toxic and carcinogenic**: long exposure damages the **bone marrow** and causes **leukaemia**; vapour causes dizziness and headache, and it passes through the skin. It is also **highly flammable**. **Precautions:** work in a fume cupboard, wear gloves, avoid skin contact and inhalation, and replace it with less harmful solvents such as **methylbenzene** where possible. **Uses:** solvent; manufacture of **styrene, phenol, aniline**, cyclohexane (for nylon), detergents (alkylbenzenes), dyes and drugs; BHC insecticide.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Electrophilic substitution: slow attack of π electrons on E⁺ gives the arenium ion; fast loss of H⁺ restores the ring.
Nitration (NO₂⁺, mixed acid), halogenation (X₂, FeX₃), sulphonation (SO₃, reversible), Friedel–Crafts alkylation (R⁺) and acylation (RCO⁺) with AlCl₃.
Directive influence: –OH, –NH₂, alkyl: o/p, activating; halogens: o/p, deactivating; –NO₂, –COOH, –CHO, –CN: meta, deactivating.
Addition (forcing): H₂/Ni to cyclohexane; Cl₂/UV to BHC. Ozonolysis: three glyoxal. Pyrolysis: biphenyl.
Benzene is carcinogenic and toxic: use a fume cupboard.

slides.narration: To sum up Part two. Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution in two steps, with the arenium ion as the intermediate. Nitration, halogenation, sulphonation and the two Friedel Crafts reactions each have a specific electrophile. Donor groups direct ortho and para and activate the ring, while withdrawing groups direct meta and deactivate it. Under forcing conditions benzene adds hydrogen or chlorine, and it can be ozonised or pyrolysed. It is a carcinogen.

sections.heading: 1. Nomenclature of aromatic compounds
sections.body_md: **Arenes** contain a benzene ring. **Monosubstituted:** substituent + benzene (chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene); special parent names include **phenol** (hydroxybenzene), **aniline** (aminobenzene), **benzoic acid**, **benzaldehyde**, **toluene** (methylbenzene) and **styrene** (ethenylbenzene). **C₆H₅–** is **phenyl**, **C₆H₅CH₂–** is **benzyl**. **Disubstituted:** **ortho (1,2), meta (1,3), para (1,4)**. **Polysubstituted:** number the ring for the **lowest locants**, cite substituents **alphabetically**, and give C-1 to the carbon bearing the group that forms the parent name (2-bromo-4-nitrobenzoic acid; 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene; 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene).

sections.heading: 2. Structure of benzene: Kekulé structures and resonance
sections.body_md: Benzene, **C₆H₆**, is a **planar regular hexagon**, all C–C **139 pm** (C–C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm), all C–C–C **120°**, C–H 109 pm. **Kekulé** drew two structures with alternating single and double bonds; benzene is a **resonance hybrid** of them (drawn as a hexagon with a circle). Each carbon is **sp²**: three σ bonds in the plane (**12 σ bonds** in all) and one p orbital perpendicular to the ring; the six p orbitals overlap to give **six delocalised π electrons**, in rings above and below the plane. **Evidence:** no decolourisation of bromine water; one C₆H₅Br; one 1,2-C₆H₄Br₂ (not two); equal bond lengths; unusual stability.

key_terms.definition_md: The real structure of a molecule that cannot be written as a single Lewis structure; it is intermediate between the contributing structures.
Spreading of π electrons over more than two atoms, which lowers the energy of the molecule.

sections.heading: 3. Stability of benzene and aromaticity
sections.body_md: **Resonance energy:** ΔH(hydrogenation) of cyclohexene = −120 kJ mol⁻¹; for three isolated C=C: 3 × (−120) = −360; observed for benzene = −208. **Resonance energy = −208 − (−360) = 152 kJ mol⁻¹** (about 150), so benzene is far more stable than a triene. **Hückel's rule:** a compound is **aromatic** if it is **planar, cyclic, fully conjugated** with **(4n + 2) π electrons** (2, 6, 10, …). Benzene 6 (n = 1), naphthalene 10 (n = 2), cyclopentadienyl anion 6, tropylium cation 6: aromatic. **Cyclobutadiene (4 π e⁻)** is antiaromatic; **cyclooctatetraene (8)** is tub-shaped and not aromatic.

key_terms.definition_md: A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated compound with (4n + 2) π electrons (Hückel's rule); unusually stable and prefers substitution to addition.
The difference in energy between the real molecule and the most stable single structure; for benzene about 150 kJ mol⁻¹.

sections.heading: 4. Preparation and physical properties
sections.body_md: **From sodium benzoate:** heat with **soda lime** (NaOH + CaO): C₆H₅COONa + NaOH → C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃ (decarboxylation). **From phenol:** pass the vapour over **heated zinc dust**: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO. (Also from ethyne through a red-hot iron tube.) **Properties:** colourless liquid, characteristic smell, bp 80.1 °C, mp 5.5 °C, density 0.879 g mL⁻¹; **insoluble in water**, miscible with organic solvents; non-polar; burns with a **sooty flame**. The melting point is high for its size because of its **symmetry** (compare methylbenzene, −95 °C; p-xylene 13 °C against o-xylene −25 °C and m-xylene −48 °C).

key_terms.definition_md: Removal of CO₂ (here as carbonate) from a carboxylate salt on heating with soda lime.

sections.heading: 5. Electrophilic substitution and its mechanism
sections.body_md: **Mechanism (two steps):** (1) slow: the π electrons attack the electrophile E⁺ to form the **arenium ion (σ complex)**, a carbocation stabilised by resonance (the + on the ortho and para carbons); (2) fast: loss of H⁺ from the sp³ carbon restores aromaticity. **Nitration:** conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, 323–333 K; electrophile **NO₂⁺** (HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻); product nitrobenzene. **Halogenation:** Cl₂ or Br₂ with FeCl₃/FeBr₃, in the dark. **Sulphonation:** conc. H₂SO₄ or oleum, electrophile **SO₃**, reversible. **Friedel–Crafts alkylation:** RCl, anhydrous AlCl₃, electrophile R⁺ (polyalkylation, rearrangement); **acylation:** RCOCl, anhydrous AlCl₃, electrophile RCO⁺, gives a ketone (C₆H₅COCH₃), no further substitution.

key_terms.definition_md: An electron-pair acceptor that attacks regions of high electron density.
The carbocation intermediate (σ complex) of electrophilic aromatic substitution, with the positive charge delocalised over three ring carbons.

sections.heading: 6. Directive influence of substituents
sections.body_md: A substituent decides the **position** and the **rate** of further substitution. **Ortho/para directors (activating):** –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃ (+M, lone pair donation) and –CH₃, –R (+I, hyperconjugation); the arenium ion for o/p attack has a resonance form with the + on the carbon bearing the donor. **Halogens:** o/p directing but **deactivating** (−I outweighs +M). **Meta directors (deactivating):** –NO₂, –CN, –COOH, –CHO, –COR, –SO₃H (−I, −M); o/p attack puts the + next to the electron-poor atom of the group, so **meta** attack is preferred. Reactivity: phenol > toluene > benzene > nitrobenzene. Nitration of toluene gives about 58% ortho, 4% meta, 38% para; nitration of nitrobenzene gives about 93% meta (1,3-dinitrobenzene).

key_terms.definition_md: A group that makes the ring react faster than benzene.
A substituent that determines the position (ortho/para or meta) taken by the next electrophile.

sections.heading: 7. Other reactions, hazards and uses
sections.body_md: **Oxidation:** benzene resists KMnO₄; burns with a sooty flame (2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O); with air and V₂O₅ at about 773 K gives maleic anhydride. **Ozonolysis:** triozonide, then Zn/H₂O gives **three glyoxal** (OHC–CHO). **Addition (forcing conditions):** H₂, Ni, 473 K gives **cyclohexane**; Cl₂ or Br₂ in **UV light (no catalyst)** gives C₆H₆Cl₆ (**BHC**, hexachlorocyclohexane) or C₆H₆Br₆. **Pyrolysis:** red-hot tube gives **biphenyl** + H₂. **Hazards:** benzene is **toxic and carcinogenic** (bone-marrow damage, leukaemia), absorbed through skin, highly flammable: use a fume cupboard, gloves, and substitute methylbenzene where possible. **Uses:** solvent; raw material for styrene, phenol, aniline, cyclohexane (nylon), detergents, dyes and drugs; BHC insecticide.

key_terms.definition_md: Benzene hexachloride, hexachlorocyclohexane C₆H₆Cl₆, formed by adding three Cl₂ to benzene in UV light; used as an insecticide.
A substance that can cause cancer; benzene causes leukaemia.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Describing benzene as a ring of three double and three single bonds that swap places (it is one resonance hybrid, all C–C 139 pm).
- Counting carbons instead of π electrons in Hückel's rule, or forgetting that the ring must be planar and conjugated.
- Writing "resonance energy = heat of hydrogenation" (it is the difference between observed and expected values).
- Giving a wrong catalyst: iron(III) chloride in the dark gives chlorobenzene; UV light with no catalyst gives BHC.
- Calling halogens meta directing (they are ortho/para directing but deactivating).
- Forgetting that Friedel–Crafts needs anhydrous AlCl₃ and that acylation stops at one substitution.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mechanism: formation of the electrophile, attack to give the arenium ion with the + shown, loss of H⁺ to the product.
- Directive effect: classify the group, say o/p or m, and justify with the resonance forms.
- Calculations: expected value, observed value, difference with sign and unit.
- Hazards: carcinogenic effect named, and one precaution.

cards.front_md: Name C₆H₅OH, C₆H₅NH₂ and C₆H₅COOH.
cards.back_md: Phenol (hydroxybenzene), aniline (aminobenzene) and benzoic acid.

cards.front_md: What are ortho, meta and para?
cards.back_md: Substituents on carbons 1,2 (ortho), 1,3 (meta) and 1,4 (para) of the ring.

cards.front_md: How are polysubstituted benzenes numbered?
cards.back_md: Lowest locants; alphabetical order of substituents; C-1 to the carbon with the group that gives the parent name.

cards.front_md: What is a phenyl group? A benzyl group?
cards.back_md: Phenyl is C₆H₅–; benzyl is C₆H₅CH₂–.

cards.front_md: Why did Kekulé structures need resonance?
cards.back_md: Two structures differ only in double-bond positions; benzene is their hybrid, with all C–C bonds equal.

cards.front_md: Length of the C–C bond in benzene?
cards.back_md: 139 pm (between 154 pm for C–C and 134 pm for C=C).

cards.front_md: Shape and bond angles of benzene?
cards.back_md: Planar regular hexagon; all angles 120°.

cards.front_md: Hybridisation of carbon in benzene and π electron count?
cards.back_md: sp²; six delocalised π electrons.

cards.front_md: Number of σ bonds in benzene?
cards.back_md: 12 (6 C–C and 6 C–H).

cards.front_md: How many 1,2-dibromobenzene isomers exist, and why is it significant?
cards.back_md: One; a Kekulé triene would give two, so the bonds must be equivalent.

cards.front_md: Calculate the resonance energy of benzene.
cards.back_md: −208 − 3(−120) = +152 kJ mol⁻¹ (about 150) more stable than a triene.

cards.front_md: State Hückel's rule.
cards.back_md: A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with (4n + 2) π electrons is aromatic.

cards.front_md: Is cyclobutadiene aromatic?
cards.back_md: No: 4 π electrons (4n) make it antiaromatic.

cards.front_md: Why is cyclooctatetraene not aromatic?
cards.back_md: It is tub-shaped, not planar, and has 8 π electrons.

cards.front_md: Benzene from sodium benzoate?
cards.back_md: Heat with soda lime: C₆H₅COONa + NaOH → C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃.

cards.front_md: Benzene from phenol?
cards.back_md: Pass phenol vapour over heated zinc dust: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO.

cards.front_md: Is benzene soluble in water? Denser or lighter?
cards.back_md: Insoluble; density 0.879 g mL⁻¹, so it floats on water.

cards.front_md: Why does benzene melt much higher than methylbenzene?
cards.back_md: Its symmetrical molecules pack closely in the crystal (5.5 °C against −95 °C).

cards.front_md: Why does benzene prefer substitution to addition?
cards.back_md: Addition would destroy the delocalised π system and its resonance energy.

cards.front_md: Electrophile in nitration of benzene?
cards.back_md: NO₂⁺ (nitronium ion) from conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄.

cards.front_md: Name the intermediate in electrophilic substitution.
cards.back_md: The arenium ion (σ complex), a resonance-stabilised carbocation.

cards.front_md: Slow and fast steps of electrophilic substitution?
cards.back_md: Slow: attack of the π electrons on E⁺; fast: loss of H⁺ to restore aromaticity.

cards.front_md: Conditions for chlorination of benzene to chlorobenzene?
cards.back_md: Cl₂ with FeCl₃ (or Fe), in the dark.

cards.front_md: Electrophile and reversibility of sulphonation?
cards.back_md: SO₃ (conc. H₂SO₄ or oleum); reversible with dilute acid or steam.

cards.front_md: Friedel–Crafts alkylation: reagent and limitations?
cards.back_md: RCl with anhydrous AlCl₃; polyalkylation and carbocation rearrangement.

cards.front_md: Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene with CH₃COCl?
cards.back_md: Gives C₆H₅COCH₃ (phenylethanone); acylium ion; no further substitution.

cards.front_md: Which groups are ortho/para directing and activating?
cards.back_md: –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃, –CH₃ and other alkyl groups.

cards.front_md: Which groups are meta directing and deactivating?
cards.back_md: –NO₂, –CN, –COOH, –CHO, –COR, –SO₃H.

cards.front_md: Halogens as directing groups?
cards.back_md: Ortho/para directing but deactivating (−I outweighs +M).

cards.front_md: Why does –NO₂ direct meta?
cards.back_md: In o/p attack the + sits next to the electron-poor N⁺; meta attack avoids this.

cards.front_md: Chlorine and benzene in UV light: product?
cards.back_md: BHC, hexachlorocyclohexane C₆H₆Cl₆ (addition, no catalyst).

cards.front_md: Health hazard of benzene and one precaution?
cards.back_md: Carcinogenic (leukaemia), toxic; work in a fume cupboard.

questions.stem_md: A dye chemist handles the compound C₆H₄(CH₃)(NO₂) in which the two groups sit on opposite corners of the ring. Its IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: Opposite corners means positions 1 and 4 (para). Substituents are cited alphabetically (methyl before nitro) and the first cited gets the lower locant: 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene — option (d). Options (a) and (b) give the wrong positions and (c) breaks the alphabetical rule.

questions.stem_md: A student draws a substituted benzoic acid: –COOH on one ring carbon, –Br on the next carbon and –NO₂ on the carbon directly opposite the –COOH. The IUPAC name is:
questions.solution_md: The carbon with –COOH is C-1. Br on the adjacent carbon is C-2 and the carbon opposite C-1 is C-4, so the name is 2-bromo-4-nitrobenzoic acid — option (b). Options (a) and (d) swap or shift the positions and (c) places the nitro group on C-5.

questions.stem_md: Which observation about benzene is directly explained by resonance between the two Kekulé structures?

options.text_md: Benzene is a liquid at room temperature
Benzene does not dissolve in water
All six carbon–carbon bonds have the same length, 139 pm
Benzene burns with a sooty flame

questions.solution_md: In a resonance hybrid, each C–C bond is partly single and partly double, so all six are equal and intermediate in length (139 pm) — option (c). Physical state (a), solubility (b) and sooty combustion (d) follow from the molecular formula and polarity, not from resonance.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene to cyclohexane is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. The resonance energy of benzene, taken from these data, is:
questions.solution_md: Expected for three isolated C=C bonds: 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Resonance energy = observed − expected = −208 − (−360) = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ — option (d). Option (a) is the difference between benzene and a single C=C, (b) is the value for two C=C bonds and (c) simply adds the two enthalpies.

questions.stem_md: How many σ bonds, and how many delocalised π electrons, are there in one molecule of benzene?
questions.solution_md: Six C–C and six C–H σ bonds give 12 σ bonds; the six unhybridised p orbitals contribute six π electrons, delocalised round the ring — option (b). Option (a) forgets the C–H bonds, (c) counts π bonds in a Kekulé structure rather than electrons and (d) overcounts the σ bonds.

questions.stem_md: Which of these species is aromatic according to Hückel's rule?
questions.solution_md: The anion has five p orbitals in a planar ring holding 6 π electrons (4n + 2 with n = 1) — option (a). The cation has 4 π electrons (4n, antiaromatic) (b), cyclobutadiene has 4 (c) and cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons and is tub-shaped, not planar (d).

questions.stem_md: In a laboratory preparation, benzene is obtained directly when which of these is heated?

options.text_md: benzoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution

questions.solution_md: Soda lime removes the carboxylate group from sodium benzoate as sodium carbonate: C₆H₅COONa + NaOH → C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃ — option (b). Sodium ethanoate gives methane (a), benzoic acid and aqueous NaOH only give the salt (c), and phenol with H₂SO₄ gives a sulphonation product (d).

questions.stem_md: Phenol vapour is passed over strongly heated zinc dust. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Zinc removes the oxygen of the –OH group as zinc oxide, leaving the ring: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO — option (d). The ring is not reduced to cyclohexane (a), no carbon is added to give methylbenzene (b), and nothing is oxidised to benzaldehyde (c).

questions.stem_md: Benzene melts at 5.5 °C, whereas methylbenzene, whose molecules are heavier, melts at −95 °C. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: benzene molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
benzene is polar but methylbenzene is non-polar
methylbenzene has weaker London forces because it is larger
benzene molecules are more symmetrical and pack more closely in the crystal

questions.solution_md: Melting depends strongly on how well molecules pack in the solid. The highly symmetrical benzene molecule fits closely in the lattice, so more energy is needed to melt it — option (d). Benzene has no O–H or N–H, so no hydrogen bonding (a); both are essentially non-polar (b); and larger molecules have stronger, not weaker, London forces (c).

questions.stem_md: Three isomeric dimethylbenzenes melt at −48 °C, −25 °C and +13 °C. The isomer that melts at +13 °C is:
questions.solution_md: The most symmetrical isomer packs best in the crystal and has the highest melting point; that is the para isomer, 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene) — option (a). The ortho (b, −25 °C) and meta (c, −48 °C) isomers are less symmetrical, and ethylbenzene (d) is not a dimethylbenzene.

questions.stem_md: Benzene is warmed with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid. The species that attacks the ring is:
questions.solution_md: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to give the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, the electrophile — option (a). The anions NO₃⁻ (b), HSO₄⁻ (c) and NO₂⁻ (d) are nucleophiles, not electrophiles.

questions.stem_md: The intermediate formed in the slow step of the nitration of benzene is best described as:

options.text_md: a free radical in which all six carbons remain sp² hybridised
an aromatic cation with six delocalised π electrons round the ring
a carbanion with the negative charge on the nitrogen atom
a resonance-stabilised carbocation in which the attacked carbon is sp³ hybridised

questions.solution_md: The π electrons form a bond to NO₂⁺, so the attacked carbon becomes sp³ and the remaining four π electrons are delocalised over five carbons, giving the arenium ion — option (d). The mechanism is ionic, not radical (a); the ion is not aromatic because the sp³ carbon breaks the ring of p orbitals (b); and the charge is positive, not negative (c).

questions.stem_md: Benzene is treated with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride. The main organic product is:
questions.solution_md: AlCl₃ generates the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺, which substitutes an H of the ring: C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl, phenylethanone — option (d). Ethylbenzene (a) would need chloroethane, chlorobenzene (b) needs Cl₂/FeCl₃ and benzoic acid (c) needs oxidation of an alkylbenzene.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the sulphonation of benzene with concentrated sulphuric acid is correct?

options.text_md: The electrophile is the HSO₄⁻ ion
The reaction needs anhydrous aluminium chloride as catalyst
It is reversible: heating benzenesulphonic acid with dilute acid or steam regenerates benzene
The product is phenyl hydrogensulphate, C₆H₅OSO₃H

questions.solution_md: Sulphonation is one of the few reversible substitutions; hydrolysis of the –SO₃H group with dilute acid or steam gives back benzene — option (c). The electrophile is SO₃ (a), no AlCl₃ is needed (b) and the sulphur is bonded to carbon, giving a sulphonic acid, not a sulphate ester (d).

questions.stem_md: Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene often gives di- and tri-alkylbenzenes, whereas acylation stops after one substitution. The reason is that:

options.text_md: acyl chlorides are far less reactive than alkyl halides
aluminium chloride is used up completely in alkylation but not in acylation
an alkyl group activates the ring towards further attack, but an acyl group deactivates it
the acylium ion is a free radical and so reacts only once

questions.solution_md: An alkyl group donates electrons, so the product is more reactive than benzene and is alkylated again; the C=O group of the acylated product withdraws electrons, so the ring is deactivated and reaction stops — option (c). Acyl chlorides are reactive enough (a), AlCl₃ is actually used in more than catalytic amounts for acylation (b) and the acylium ion is a cation, not a radical (d).

questions.stem_md: A second substituent enters mainly at the meta position when the compound being nitrated is:
questions.solution_md: The –NO₂ group withdraws electrons and directs meta (about 93% 1,3-dinitrobenzene) — option (a). –OH (b) and –CH₃ (c) are ortho/para directing activators, and chlorine (d) is ortho/para directing though deactivating.

questions.stem_md: Benzene, nitrobenzene, phenol and methylbenzene are each nitrated under the same mild conditions. The order of decreasing rate is:
questions.solution_md: The –OH group is a strong activator (+M), –CH₃ a weak activator (+I and hyperconjugation), and –NO₂ a strong deactivator (−I, −M): phenol > methylbenzene > benzene > nitrobenzene — option (c). Option (a) is the exact reverse; (b) and (d) misplace the weak or the strong activator.

questions.stem_md: Nitration of chlorobenzene gives mainly 2- and 4-nitrochlorobenzene, yet it is slower than the nitration of benzene. This is because chlorine:

options.text_md: is a meta director that deactivates the ring
donates electrons both inductively and by resonance, so it activates the ring
withdraws electrons inductively, which deactivates the ring, but donates a lone pair by resonance to the ortho and para positions
has no lone pair and so cannot take part in resonance

questions.solution_md: Chlorine is very electronegative (−I effect), which makes the ring less reactive overall; its lone pairs are donated into the ring (+M) and stabilise the arenium ion formed by ortho or para attack, so substitution goes there — option (c). Chlorine is not a meta director (a), does not activate (b) and has three lone pairs (d).

questions.stem_md: Methylbenzene is mononitrated with mixed acid in a small-scale experiment. Which pair of products makes up most of the mixture?
questions.solution_md: The methyl group is ortho/para directing, so the main products are the 2- (about 58%) and 4- (about 38%) isomers — option (a). Only about 4% of the meta isomer forms, so (b), (c) and (d) all include the minor 3-isomer.

questions.stem_md: Benzene vapour and hydrogen are passed over finely divided nickel at 473 K. The product is:
questions.solution_md: All three π bonds add H₂: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂, cyclohexane — option (b). The reaction does not stop at cyclohexene (a), the ring is not opened to hexane (c) and the ring size does not change (d).

questions.stem_md: Chlorine is bubbled through boiling benzene in bright sunlight, without any catalyst. The compound formed is:
questions.solution_md: In UV light, chlorine adds to the ring by a radical mechanism: C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆, hexachlorocyclohexane (BHC) — option (c). Substitution products (a, b, d) need a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ in the dark.

questions.stem_md: Benzene is treated with ozone and the ozonide is then decomposed with zinc and water. The organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Each of the three C=C bonds of a Kekulé structure is cleaved, and each carbon becomes a CHO group, so the six carbons give three OHC–CHO molecules — option (b). Ethanal (a) would have a CH₃ group that benzene lacks, the acid (c) needs an oxidising work-up and methanal (d) would need the C–C bonds to break as well.

questions.stem_md: Which long-term health effect is most strongly linked with breathing benzene vapour over many years?

options.text_md: damage to the bone marrow, leading to leukaemia

questions.solution_md: Benzene is a proven human carcinogen; chronic exposure damages blood-forming bone marrow and can cause leukaemia — option (b). Silicosis (a) comes from silica dust, cataract (c) from ultraviolet exposure among other causes, and goitre (d) from iodine deficiency.

questions.stem_md: Benzene vapour is passed through a tube heated to redness. Besides hydrogen, the organic product is:
questions.solution_md: Two benzene molecules join through a C–C bond with loss of H₂: 2C₆H₆ → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + H₂, biphenyl — option (a). Diphenylmethane (b) would need an extra carbon, naphthalene (c) has two fused rings and cyclohexane (d) is the hydrogenation product.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Benzene does not decolourise bromine water under ordinary conditions.

**Reason (R):** The delocalised π electrons give benzene a large resonance energy, which addition reactions would destroy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: addition would break the delocalised π system and lose about 150 kJ mol⁻¹, so benzene prefers substitution and does not react with bromine water — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The nitration of benzene is carried out with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulphuric acid.

**Reason (R):** Benzene is less dense than water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. The acid mixture is used because it generates the NO₂⁺ electrophile; the density of benzene has nothing to do with the choice of reagents, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Further nitration of nitrobenzene gives mainly 1,3-dinitrobenzene.

**Reason (R):** The nitro group donates electrons to the ring by resonance and so activates it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the nitro group withdraws electrons by the −I and −M effects, which deactivates the ring and directs the next substituent to the meta position — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Benzene has three localised C=C bonds and three C–C bonds of different lengths, 134 pm and 154 pm.

**Reason (R):** Benzene has four π electrons, which is a Hückel number.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: all six C–C bonds are equal (139 pm) because the π electrons are delocalised, and benzene has six π electrons (4n + 2 with n = 1); four π electrons would be 4n and antiaromatic — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene gives only the monoacyl product, even with an excess of acyl chloride.

**Reason (R):** The acyl group is an electron-donating group that activates the ring towards further substitution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the C=O group withdraws electrons and deactivates the ring, which is why a second acylation does not occur — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Heating phenol vapour with zinc dust gives benzene.

**Reason (R):** Benzene is classified as a human carcinogen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Zinc removes the oxygen of phenol as ZnO; the carcinogenicity of benzene has no bearing on how it is prepared, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All twelve atoms of a benzene molecule lie in one plane, and every C–C–C angle is 120°.
questions.solution_md: True. Each carbon is sp² hybridised, so the six carbons form a regular planar hexagon and each hydrogen lies in the same plane.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The –OH group of phenol directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the meta position.
questions.solution_md: False. –OH donates a lone pair to the ring (+M effect), stabilising the arenium ion for ortho and para attack, so it is an ortho/para director and strongly activating.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When benzene reacts with chlorine in the dark in the presence of iron(III) chloride, the main product is hexachlorocyclohexane.
questions.solution_md: False. With a Lewis acid catalyst in the dark, substitution occurs and chlorobenzene is formed; hexachlorocyclohexane forms only by addition in UV light without a catalyst.

questions.stem_md: A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring is aromatic if it contains (4n + 2) π electrons; benzene contains ___ π electrons.
questions.solution_md: **6** π electrons (n = 1).

questions.stem_md: The electrophile in the sulphonation of benzene with oleum is ___.
questions.solution_md: **SO₃** (sulphur trioxide).

questions.stem_md: On pyrolysis, two molecules of benzene join with loss of hydrogen to give ___.
questions.solution_md: **Biphenyl**, C₆H₅–C₆H₅.

questions.stem_md: Match each electrophilic substitution of benzene in Column I with the electrophile that attacks the ring in Column II.

options.text_md: Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl and AlCl₃

questions.solution_md: Mixed acid makes the nitronium ion; oleum supplies SO₃; AlCl₃ turns the acid chloride into the acylium ion; FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂ so that it behaves as Cl⁺.

questions.stem_md: Match each substituent on a benzene ring in Column I with its directing and activating effect in Column II.
questions.solution_md: –OH donates by resonance and strongly activates; –NO₂ withdraws by −I and −M and directs meta; halogens withdraw inductively but donate by resonance (o/p, deactivating); –CH₃ activates weakly through +I and hyperconjugation.

questions.stem_md: Complete hydrogenation of one mole of benzene to cyclohexane releases 208 kJ of heat. How much heat, in kJ, is released when 3.90 g of benzene is hydrogenated completely? (C = 12, H = 1)

questions.stem_md: Using Hückel's rule, decide whether (i) cyclobutadiene, (ii) the cyclopentadienyl anion and (iii) naphthalene are aromatic, giving the number of π electrons in each. Assume each is planar.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Cyclobutadiene has 4 π electrons, which is 4n (n = 1), so it is antiaromatic, not aromatic. (ii) The cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 π electrons (four from two double bonds and two from the lone pair on the sp² carbon), which is 4n + 2 with n = 1: aromatic. (iii) Naphthalene has 10 π electrons (4n + 2 with n = 2): aromatic.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpies of hydrogenation to cyclohexane are: cyclohexene −120, cyclohexa-1,4-diene −240 and benzene −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the stabilisation (resonance energy) of benzene and the same quantity for cyclohexa-1,4-diene, and explain why the two values differ so much.

answer.model_answer_md: Benzene: expected 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹; resonance energy = −208 − (−360) = 152 kJ mol⁻¹. Cyclohexa-1,4-diene: expected 2 × (−120) = −240 kJ mol⁻¹; stabilisation = −240 − (−240) = 0 kJ mol⁻¹. In the 1,4-diene the two double bonds are isolated (separated by CH₂ groups), so their π electrons cannot be delocalised and there is no extra stability, whereas in benzene all six π electrons are delocalised round a closed, cyclic arrangement (aromatic stability), which lowers its energy by about 150 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: Benzene 152 kJ mol⁻¹; cyclohexa-1,4-diene 0; cyclic delocalisation of six π electrons only in benzene.

marking_scheme.step: Isolated double bonds cannot delocalise; cyclic delocalisation of six π electrons in benzene

questions.stem_md: Describe the mechanism of the nitration of benzene: show how the electrophile is formed, the intermediate that results from the attack on the ring, and the step that gives nitrobenzene.

answer.model_answer_md: The electrophile forms in the acid mixture: $\ce{HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-}$. Step 1 (slow): the π electrons of benzene attack NO₂⁺, forming the arenium ion, a carbocation in which the attacked carbon is sp³ (bearing H and NO₂) and the + charge is spread over the ortho and para carbons by resonance. Step 2 (fast): HSO₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, the π system is restored and nitrobenzene forms.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the preparation of ethylbenzene from benzene and bromoethane by the Friedel–Crafts method, naming the catalyst and the electrophile, and give one limitation of the method.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{C6H6 + C2H5Br ->[AlCl3] C6H5C2H5 + HBr}$. The catalyst is anhydrous aluminium chloride, which helps to form the ethyl carbocation, C₂H₅⁺, the electrophile. A limitation is polyalkylation: the ethyl group activates the ring, so diethyl- and triethylbenzenes also form (or, for longer chains, the carbocation can rearrange).

questions.stem_md: Benzene is converted into phenylethanone by Friedel–Crafts acylation. Write the equation, name the electrophile, and explain why the reaction stops after one acyl group has entered although alkylation often does not.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$. The electrophile is the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺. The carbonyl group of the product withdraws electrons from the ring (−I, −M), deactivating it, so it is less reactive than benzene and a second acylation does not occur; an alkyl group in alkylation donates electrons and activates the ring, so further substitution happens.

questions.stem_md: Nitrobenzene is nitrated mainly at the meta position and more slowly than benzene. Explain both facts by considering the arenium ion formed on attack at the ortho and at the meta position.

answer.model_answer_md: The nitro group withdraws electrons (−I and −M), so the ring is less able to stabilise the positive charge of the arenium ion and reacts more slowly than benzene. In ortho (and para) attack, one resonance form of the ion has the positive charge on the carbon directly attached to the N⁺ of the nitro group; two positive charges on adjacent atoms is very unfavourable. In meta attack the + is never on that carbon, so this form is avoided; the meta ion is the least unstable, and meta substitution is preferred.

Meta attack avoids this, so it is preferred

(a) Draw the two Kekulé structures of benzene and explain why benzene is described as a resonance hybrid. [2]

(b) Describe the orbital structure of benzene: the hybridisation of carbon, the σ bonds and the π system. [2]

(c) State Hückel's rule and show that benzene obeys it. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The two structures are hexagons with alternating double and single bonds, differing only in the positions of the double bonds. Neither alone fits the facts (all C–C bonds equal, 139 pm); the real molecule is a hybrid of both, with the π electrons delocalised, and is more stable than either. (b) Each carbon is sp² hybridised and forms three σ bonds (two C–C and one C–H) in one plane at 120°, giving 12 σ bonds; the unhybridised p orbital on each carbon, perpendicular to the ring, overlaps sideways with its neighbours, forming a delocalised π cloud of 6 electrons above and below the ring. (c) A planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with (4n + 2) π electrons is aromatic; benzene has 6 π electrons, which is 4n + 2 with n = 1.
